canonicalName: Topology from the geometry of position (Euler to Listing)

milestones.label: Euler's Konigsberg bridges paper published
milestones.work: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis, Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petropol. 8, pp. 128-140 (volume dated 1736, published 1741; written 1735), E53
milestones.description: Euler solved the bridge problem by pure connectivity and said in the title that it belongs to a geometry where measure plays no role.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E53 lists publication 1741, written 1735, journal vol. 8 pp. 128-140.
MacTutor notes the title shows Euler knew this was a different geometry in which distance is irrelevant.

milestones.note: MacTutor dates the paper 1736 (the volume year); the Euler Archive gives 1741 as publication year. 1741 used per rule that publication governs.

milestones.label: Euler's polyhedron formula papers
milestones.work: Euler, Elementa doctrinae solidorum, Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petropol. 4, pp. 109-140 (1758; written 1750), E230
milestones.description: Euler set out the relation between vertices, edges and faces of a polyhedron, the second measurement-free result of the field.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E230: published 1758, written 1750, Novi Commentarii vol. 4 pp. 109-140.
Wikipedia Euler characteristic: concept originally defined for polyhedra; Euler gave the polyhedron relation.

milestones.label: Lhuilier's genus correction of Euler's formula
milestones.work: Lhuilier, Memoire sur la polyedrometrie..., Annales de mathematiques pures et appliquees 3 (1812-1813), pp. 169-189
milestones.description: Lhuilier showed that Euler's relation fails for solids with holes and corrected it to 2 - 2g, bringing in the genus.

evidence.claim: Numdam record: Annales de mathematiques pures et appliquees, Tome 3 (1812-1813), pp. 169-189, with examination of exceptions to Euler's theorem.
MacTutor says Lhuilier noticed Euler's formula fails for solids with holes and gave v - e + f = 2 - 2g in 1813.

milestones.note: Volume dated 1812-13; MacTutor says 1813. A separate 1811 St Petersburg memoir by Lhuilier was not verified.

milestones.label: Listing coins 'topology' in a letter
milestones.description: Listing used the word topology in a private letter to his former teacher, not yet in print.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says the word topology first appears in a long letter to his school teacher written on the Sicily journey, and dates its first use to 1836.

milestones.note: Exact letter date not given by sources read (Sicily trip began mid-1834; MacTutor text says 1836).

milestones.label: Listing's Vorstudien zur Topologie
milestones.work: Listing, Vorstudien zur Topologie, Gottinger Studien 1847 (separate print Gottingen, Vandenhoeck und Ruprecht, 1848)
milestones.description: The word topology appeared in print for the first time in this essay, which defines it as the study of connection and position without regard to measure.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the book dated 1848 (Vandenhoeck und Ruprecht).
MacTutor says Listing wrote the Vorstudien in 1847 and that it was the first printed use of the word.
Wikipedia Topology: introduced the term in Vorstudien zur Topologie, 1847.

milestones.note: 1847 is the date of the essay in Gottinger Studien; the stand-alone print is dated 1848. The Gottinger Studien volume itself was not checked in a catalogue.

milestones.label: Leibniz's geometry of position (idea only)
milestones.description: Leibniz imagined a geometry of position (geometria situs, analysis situs) in the seventeenth century, before any worked topological result.

evidence.claim: Topology article says the ideas go back to Leibniz's geometria situs and analysis situs in the 17th century.

milestones.note: Year not established from the pages read; searched Wikipedia Topology and MacTutor Topology in mathematics only. Kept as an undated precursor.

works.citation: Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis (E53)
works.whyItMatters: First worked problem treated by connectivity alone.
Relation among vertices, edges and faces.

people.name: Simon Lhuilier

works.citation: Memoire sur la polyedrometrie, Ann. math. pures appl. 3

people.roleNote: Corrected Euler's formula for solids with holes

people.name: Johann Benedict Listing

works.whyItMatters: First printed use of the word.

people.roleNote: Coined 'topology' and wrote the first book-length preliminary study

notes: Poincare's Analysis Situs (1895) and later combinatorial topology are outside the Euler-to-Listing span and not listed. The summary's claim that the name was 'fixed in 1847' is supported only as 'first used in print in 1847'; English 'topology' came later (Wikipedia gives 1883). Leibniz precursor left undated. Searched: Euler Archive, Numdam, Crossref (no usable old records), Internet Archive, MacTutor topic and biography pages.

milestones.label: Seki's Hatsubi Sanpo solves 15 problems by elimination
milestones.work: Seki Takakazu, Hatsubi Sanpo, 1674
milestones.description: Seki gave single-variable equations that result from elimination for fifteen set problems, but did not reveal the process.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says Seki published Hatsubi Sanpo in 1674 solving fifteen problems posed four years earlier.
Wikipedia says the 1674 book gave only the resulting single-variable equations with no account of the process or symbols.

milestones.note: No bibliographic record found; searched Internet Archive and Crossref only.

milestones.label: Kaifukudai no Ho: resultant and determinant in manuscript
milestones.work: Seki Takakazu, Kaifukudai no Ho, 1683 (manuscript)
milestones.description: Seki pushed elimination theory using resultants and devised determinants to express them, in a manuscript whose 5x5 formula was wrong.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: in 1683 Seki developed the determinant to express the resultant in Kaifukudai no Ho; the 5x5 formula in the manuscript is wrong.
MacTutor: Seki was the first person to study determinants, in 1683, ten years before Leibniz.

milestones.note: Circulated in a closed school as a manuscript, so treated as a precursor under the private-versus-public rule rather than a public first statement.

milestones.label: Taisei Sankei compiled: complete determinant formula
milestones.work: Seki, Takebe brothers, Taisei Sankei (compiled 1683-1710)
milestones.description: The school's encyclopaedia, assembled over decades, contains a correct general determinant expansion.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: Taisei Sankei, written 1683-1710, contains a correct general formula equivalent to Laplace's expansion; the complete version is no later than 1710.
MacTutor biography of Takebe: Seki's project to record mathematics launched 1683, carried on by the Takebe brothers.

milestones.note: Manuscript compilation; range, not a publication date.

milestones.label: Takebe's Hatsubi Sanpo Genkai shows elimination in detail
milestones.work: Takebe Katahiro, Hatsubi Sanpo Genkai, 1685
milestones.description: A pupil of Seki published notes showing the elimination process in full using the new algebraic symbols, the first open account of the method.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: in 1685 Takebe Katahiro published notes on Hatsubi Sanpo showing the process of elimination in detail with algebraic symbols.

milestones.note: Earliest public statement found; Seki's own priority rests on manuscripts. Tanaka Yoshizane's 1678 Sanpo Meiki appears to contain related elimination results; not checked against a primary source.

people.name: Takakazu Seki
people.roleNote: Developed elimination via resultants and determinants

people.name: Katahiro Takebe

works.whyItMatters: Published the elimination process in detail.

people.roleNote: Pupil who published the elimination method and co-wrote Taisei Sankei

works.citation: Determinants used for simultaneous equations (per MacTutor, ten years after Seki)

notes: The summary says Seki 'found resultant and determinant'; sources agree on 1683 but only as manuscript, with a flawed 5x5 formula, and a complete version by 1710 in a school compilation. Tanaka Yoshizane is credited by Wikipedia with an independent explicit resultant (Sanpo Funkai, c.1690?) - uncertain date, left out of milestones. No bibliographic records exist for these Japanese manuscripts in Crossref or Internet Archive; all evidence is history pages. No naming or institution milestone applicable (pre-MSC).

canonicalName: Calculus of variations from the brachistochrone

milestones.label: Newton's minimal resistance problem in the Principia
milestones.work: Newton, Philosophiae naturalis principia mathematica, 1687
milestones.description: Newton formulated and solved the solid of least resistance, an extremum problem over curves, but not as part of a general method.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, Calculus of variations: Newton's minimal resistance problem, formulated 1685 and published in the Principia 1687, was the first correctly solved problem of the field.
Internet Archive holds the 1687 first edition.

milestones.note: Whether this counts as the start of the field is disputed; kept as precursor.

milestones.label: Johann Bernoulli poses the brachistochrone problem
milestones.work: Johann Bernoulli, Problema novum..., Acta Eruditorum, June 1696
milestones.description: Bernoulli publicly challenged mathematicians to find the curve of quickest descent, the problem that opened the field.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: the problem was posed by Johann Bernoulli in Acta Eruditorum in June 1696.

milestones.note: No Crossref/zbMATH record exists for Acta Eruditorum 1696; searched Crossref.

milestones.label: Solutions to the brachistochrone published in Acta Eruditorum
milestones.work: Acta Eruditorum, May 1697 (Leibniz p. 205, Johann Bernoulli pp. 206-211, Jakob Bernoulli pp. 211-214, Newton p. 223)
milestones.description: Five solutions were obtained and four appeared in print in May 1697; Jakob Bernoulli's approach already treated the curve as an unknown to be varied.

evidence.claim: MacTutor lists the May 1697 Acta Eruditorum contents with page numbers of each solution.

milestones.label: Euler's Methodus inveniendi
milestones.work: Euler, Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas maximi minimive proprietate gaudentes, Lausanne and Geneva 1744 (written 1743), E65
milestones.description: Euler turned a set of special cases into a general method, gave a first-order necessary condition (the Euler differential equation) and treated about a hundred problems.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E65: quarto book published 1744, written 1743; summary describes the general procedure and 100 problems.
MacTutor Euler biography credits the Methodus with beginning the proper study of the subject.

milestones.note: MacTutor says 1740; the Euler Archive gives 1744 (written 1743). 1744 used.

milestones.label: Lagrange's analytic method with the delta symbol
milestones.work: Lagrange, Essai d'une nouvelle methode pour determiner les maxima et les minima des formules integrales indefinies, Miscellanea Taurinensia 2 (1760-61, published 1762)
milestones.description: Lagrange replaced Euler's partly geometric reasoning by a purely analytic one based on variations of the function; Euler adopted it.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia (citing Thiele and Goldstine): Euler dropped his geometric approach for Lagrange's analytic one after seeing his 1755 work, and waited until Lagrange published in 1762.
MacTutor Lagrange: results sent to Euler in August 1755 contributed to the new subject.

milestones.note: Publication year 1762 taken from a secondary page; the Turin volume was not located in a catalogue. The 1755 letter to Euler is a private precursor.

milestones.label: Euler's Elementa calculi variationum
milestones.work: Euler, Elementa calculi variationum, Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petropol. 10 (1766; read 1756), E296
milestones.description: Euler gave the subject its name in the title of a treatise written in 1756 and printed ten years later.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E296: published 1766, written 1756; read to the Berlin Academy on 16 September 1756.
MacTutor Lagrange: the name 'calculus of variations' was given by Euler in 1766.

milestones.note: Wikipedia dates the renaming to the 1756 lecture; the printed title is 1766.

people.name: Jakob Bernoulli
people.roleNote: Solved the brachistochrone and posed isoperimetric problems

notes: The summary's attribution of the 'delta symbol' to Lagrange rests on Wikipedia/MacTutor wording, not on a primary text I checked. Jakob Bernoulli's 1701 isoperimetric solution and Euler's earlier E9 (1732) and E27 (1738) were not made milestones. Mixed type 'birth-by-fusion' is plausible but not tested here. Searched: MacTutor, Euler Archive, Internet Archive, Crossref (no records for Acta Eruditorum or Turin volumes).

canonicalName: Trigonometry and the exponential: Cotes, De Moivre, Euler

milestones.label: Johann Bernoulli links inverse sine and logarithm
milestones.work: Johann Bernoulli, work of 1702 on integration (Memoires de l'Academie des Sciences, Paris)
milestones.description: Bernoulli related the inverse sine of an argument to a logarithm of a complex expression, the first link between angle functions and logarithms.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Johann Bernoulli found the relation between the inverse sine and the logarithm in 1702.

milestones.note: Specific paper not identified or checked in a bibliographic record; year taken from MacTutor only.

milestones.label: Cotes's Logometria
milestones.work: Cotes, Logometria, Philosophical Transactions 29 (338), pp. 5-45, March 1714
milestones.description: Cotes gave a geometric statement equivalent to ix = log(cos x + i sin x), up to a misplaced factor of i.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Logometria, Phil. Trans. 29, pp. 5-45, dated 1714.
Wikipedia, De Moivre's formula and Roger Cotes: the 1714 argument, once a misplaced factor is corrected, is equivalent to the logarithmic form of Euler's formula.

milestones.note: MacTutor dates this result to 1722, the posthumous Harmonia mensurarum, which reprinted Logometria; the 1714 paper is earlier.

milestones.label: De Moivre's power formula
milestones.work: De Moivre, paper of 1722 (candidate: De sectione anguli, Phil. Trans. 32, pp. 228-230)
milestones.description: De Moivre published the rule for powers of cos x + i sin x, taking angle multiplication into complex arithmetic.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: De Moivre published the theorem in 1722; a closely related formula appeared in an earlier paper of 1707.

milestones.note: The exact paper was not confirmed. Crossref lists 'De sectione anguli' (Phil. Trans. 32, 1722) as a candidate, kept out of the evidence. Wikipedia says the explicit form came in Miscellanea analytica (1730).

milestones.label: Euler turns to the exponential and corresponds with Bernoulli
milestones.description: Around 1740 Euler compared the series for the exponential and the trigonometric functions; in letters with Bernoulli he also suggested logarithms have infinitely many values.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, Euler's formula: around 1740 Euler derived the relation by comparing series; his correspondence with Bernoulli shows Bernoulli did not grasp complex logarithms and Euler suggested infinitely many values.

milestones.note: Private work; date approximate.

milestones.label: Euler publishes exp(ix) = cos x + i sin x
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, vol. 1, Lausanne 1748 (written 1745), E101
milestones.description: The exponential form of the formula appears in print in the first volume of the Introductio.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E101: quarto book published 1748, written 1745.
MacTutor: Euler in 1748 gave the formula exp(ix) = cos x + i sin x, equivalent to Cotes's.

milestones.label: Introductio makes the function central to analysis
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, 1748, E101
milestones.description: The same book also gives the first systematic treatment of elementary functions, series and exponentials as the base of analysis.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive summary of E101: lays the foundations of modern analysis, centres the function concept and the role of e^x.

milestones.note: Same work as the previous milestone; it truly plays both roles (first printing of the formula and first systematic treatment).

milestones.label: Euler settles the logarithms of negative numbers
milestones.work: Euler, De la controverse entre Mrs. Leibnitz et Bernoulli sur les logarithmes des nombres negatifs et imaginaires, Mem. Acad. Berlin 5, pp. 139-179 (1751; written 1747), E168
milestones.description: Euler resolved the old Leibniz-Bernoulli dispute by showing that logarithms of complex numbers are many-valued.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E168: published 1751, written 1747, Berlin Memoires vol. 5 pp. 139-179.

milestones.note: The 'many-valued' description of the paper's conclusion is standard but not stated in the Euler Archive record; Wikipedia Euler's formula supports the infinitely-many-values point.

people.name: Roger Cotes

works.whyItMatters: Geometric form of ix = log(cos x + i sin x).

people.roleNote: Logarithm of cos x + i sin x

notes: Priority is disputed: MacTutor dates Cotes to 1722 (Harmonia mensurarum) while the Crossref record shows Logometria in 1714; MacTutor and Wikipedia also differ on whether De Moivre's explicit formula is 1722 or 1730. The summary's 'Euler gave exp(ix)' is supported for the 1748 print but Euler's own private derivation is dated only 'around 1740'. Bernoulli 1702 has no bibliographic record found.

canonicalName: De Moivre's formula: trigonometry and complex powers

milestones.label: De Moivre's cubic and higher-degree root formula
milestones.work: De Moivre, Aequationum quarundam potestatis tertiae, quintae, septimae, nonae... resolutio analytica, Phil. Trans. 25 (309), pp. 2368-2371, 1707
milestones.description: A closely related relation between multiples of an angle appears in an earlier paper on solving equations by series.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Phil. Trans. 25, pp. 2368-2371, dated 1707.
MacTutor: a closely related formula appeared in an earlier paper of 1707.

milestones.note: Identification of the 1707 paper with MacTutor's remark follows Wikipedia's citation; the content was not read.

milestones.label: Cotes's geometric logarithm statement
milestones.work: Cotes, Logometria, Phil. Trans. 29, pp. 5-45, 1714
milestones.description: An equivalent logarithmic statement for the angle, which implies the power rule, appeared eight years earlier.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Logometria, Phil. Trans. 29, 1714.
Wikipedia, De Moivre's formula: Cotes's 1714 argument, corrected for a misplaced factor, gives ix = ln(cos x + i sin x).

milestones.label: De Moivre's formula appears in a Philosophical Transactions paper
milestones.work: De Moivre, paper of 1722 (candidate: De sectione anguli, Phil. Trans. 32, pp. 228-230)
milestones.description: MacTutor says the formula for (cos x + i sin x)^n first appears in this exact form in a paper of 1722.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: the formula appears in this form in a paper that De Moivre published in 1722.

milestones.note: Exact paper unconfirmed; Crossref candidate 'De sectione anguli' (1722) not read. Wikipedia instead cites Miscellanea analytica (1730) for the explicit lemma, so priority between 1722 and 1730 is open.

milestones.label: Miscellanea analytica states the multiple-angle lemma
milestones.work: De Moivre, Miscellanea analytica de seriebus et quadraturis, London: Tonson and Watts, 1730
milestones.description: Wikipedia cites the first page of this book for De Moivre's explicit lemma on cosines of an angle and its multiples.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the 1730 London edition.
Wikipedia, De Moivre's formula: in 1730 De Moivre explicitly considered cos of an angle and its integer multiple (p. 1).

milestones.label: Euler's exponential form
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, vol. 1, 1748, E101
milestones.description: Euler's formula exp(ix) = cos x + i sin x contains the power rule as an exponent law and replaced De Moivre's trigonometric form in practice.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E101: published 1748.
MacTutor: Euler gave exp(ix) = cos x + i sin x in 1748.

notes: The date of first statement is genuinely disputed between sources (1707 related, 1722 per MacTutor, 1730 per Wikipedia, 1714 by Cotes in a different form). No naming milestone found: when 'de Moivre's formula' became the usual name was not established. Derived conceptual date 1722 is a low-certainty choice.

canonicalName: Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi and the law of large numbers

milestones.label: Pascal-Fermat correspondence
milestones.description: Letters on the problem of points are the date historians cite for the start of modern probability.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, Ars Conjectandi: historians cite the Pascal-Fermat correspondence of 1654 as the beginning of modern probability.

milestones.note: Private correspondence.

milestones.label: Huygens's treatise on reckoning in games of chance
milestones.work: Huygens, De ratiociniis in ludo aleae, in van Schooten, Exercitationum mathematicarum libri quinque, Leiden 1657
milestones.description: The first printed treatise on probability, built on expectation for games of chance.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the 1657 printing of De ratiociniis in ludo aleae.
Wikipedia, Ars Conjectandi, describes Huygens as having published the first treatise on probability.

milestones.note: Consolidation of the earlier stage, before the Bernoulli work this event names.

milestones.label: Jakob Bernoulli's Meditationes notebook
milestones.work: Jakob Bernoulli, Meditationes (private notes), 1684-1689
milestones.description: Bernoulli's private notebook records three working periods from games of chance to a posteriori probabilities and the measuring of probabilities.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, Ars Conjectandi: the Meditationes show progress in three periods, 1684-85, 1685-86 and 1687-89; text written 1684-1689.

milestones.note: Unpublished notes.

milestones.label: Ars Conjectandi published
milestones.work: Jakob Bernoulli, Ars conjectandi, opus posthumum, Basel: Thurneysen, 1713
milestones.description: The posthumous book contains the first version of the law of large numbers and a systematic treatment of combinatorics and expectation.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the 1713 Basel edition (several scans).
MacTutor: Ars Conjectandi published in Basel in 1713, eight years after Bernoulli's death.

milestones.note: Published eight years after his death; MacTutor loosely says he 'published' the law by 1689, but the printed statement is 1713. The book also consolidates probability and combinatorics; no second milestone created.

milestones.label: De Moivre's Doctrine of Chances
milestones.work: De Moivre, The Doctrine of Chances, London 1718
milestones.description: De Moivre's English treatise extended the calculus of chances after Bernoulli's book; his 1711 De mensura sortis preceded it.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the 1718 first edition.
Wikipedia, Ars Conjectandi, notes the book influenced de Moivre.

milestones.note: Relevance to this event is the follow-up, not the origin; his 1711 De mensura sortis (Crossref 10.1098/rstl.1710.0018) is a related candidate.

works.whyItMatters: Law of large numbers and combinatorics.

notes: The input summary 'proved the first law of large numbers' is consistent with Wikipedia ('very first version') but the proof is in the posthumous book, with composition dated 1684-1689 by Wikipedia's account of the Meditationes; the date of the actual proof was not established. The Latin edition is also catalogued under 1713 with later reprints. No naming or institution milestone applies (pre-MSC; Nicolaus Bernoulli 1713 correspondence with Montmort not checked). Montmort's 1708 Essay was searched on Internet Archive and not found, so left out.

canonicalName: Taylor: finite differences and Taylor's theorem

milestones.label: Gregory's earlier series result
milestones.description: Gregory had a version of the expansion in 1671, as Wikipedia puts it, an earlier version mentioned in his work.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, Taylor's theorem: named after Taylor who stated a version in 1715, though an earlier version was mentioned by James Gregory in 1671.

milestones.note: Specific Gregory text not identified. MacTutor Taylor also lists Newton, Leibniz, Johann Bernoulli and de Moivre as independent discoverers of variants.

milestones.label: Taylor's letter to Machin
milestones.description: In a letter of 26 July 1712 Taylor first mentioned a version of the theorem, prompted by a remark of Machin about Newton's series and Halley's root method.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Taylor biography gives the letter date and the coffee-house origin of the idea.

milestones.note: Private letter.

milestones.label: Methodus incrementorum directa et inversa
milestones.work: Taylor, Methodus incrementorum directa et inversa, London 1715 (2nd ed. 1717)
milestones.description: The book founded the calculus of finite differences and contains two forms of what is now called Taylor's series.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the 1715 edition.
MacTutor: the 1715 book contains the Taylor series, and gave a new branch now called the calculus of finite differences.

milestones.note: Truly both the first statement of the series and of the finite-difference calculus under one name; one milestone only.

milestones.label: Stirling's Methodus differentialis
milestones.work: Stirling, Methodus differentialis, sive tractatus de summatione et interpolatione serierum infinitarum, London 1730
milestones.description: A treatise on summation and interpolation of series by differences, the next major book in the same tradition.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive holds the 1730 London edition.

milestones.note: Relevance to Taylor's calculus rests on the title only; content not read. A 1717 Stirling commentary on Newton's differential method also exists on Internet Archive.

milestones.label: Name 'Taylor series' in use
milestones.description: MacTutor says the series only came to be called Taylor's in 1785.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: the series is the Taylor series, though it only became known as this in 1785.

milestones.note: Date of coinage from one history page, source work not identified; earlier uses were not searched.

works.whyItMatters: Calculus of finite differences and Taylor series.

notes: The summary treats Taylor as the creator of the finite-difference calculus; MacTutor agrees that the book 'added' this branch but lists several independent earlier variants of the series (Gregory, Newton, Leibniz, Johann Bernoulli, de Moivre). Newton's Methodus differentialis (1711) was not checked. Maclaurin and the later rigorous remainder estimates were not researched. No Crossref entry for the 1715 book.

milestones.label: Johann Bernoulli on inverse sine and logarithm
milestones.description: Bernoulli's 1702 relation between inverse sine and logarithm preceded Euler's treatment.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Bernoulli found the relation between inverse sine and logarithm in 1702.

milestones.note: Specific paper not identified.

milestones.label: Cotes's Logometria
milestones.work: Cotes, Logometria, Phil. Trans. 29, pp. 5-45, 1714
milestones.description: Cotes already had the logarithm of cos x + i sin x in geometric form.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Logometria, Phil. Trans. 29, 1714.

milestones.label: Euler publishes the exponential-trigonometric relation
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, vol. 1, 1748, E101
milestones.description: Euler's first book on analysis prints exp(ix) = cos x + i sin x and the exponential as the base of the elementary functions.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E101: published 1748.
Wikipedia, Euler's formula: first published in 1748 in the Introductio.

milestones.label: Euler on the logarithms of negative and imaginary numbers
milestones.work: Euler, De la controverse entre Mrs. Leibnitz et Bernoulli..., Mem. Acad. Berlin 5, pp. 139-179, 1751 (written 1747), E168
milestones.description: The paper treats the dispute over the logarithm of negative numbers; Euler held that logarithms are multi-valued.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E168: published 1751, written 1747.
Wikipedia, Euler's formula: Euler suggested complex logarithms have infinitely many values.

people.name: Leonhard Euler
people.roleNote: Exponential and logarithm of complex numbers

people.name: Johann Bernoulli
people.roleNote: Inverse sine-logarithm link; party to the dispute

notes: Same underlying history as H76 but centred on Euler. The summary 'logarithms of negatives' is represented by the 1751 paper; the Leibniz side of the controversy (Acta Eruditorum 1712-13) was not verified. The complex-analysis target named in the input is not itself tied to a dated milestone here.

milestones.label: Euler on the shortest line on a surface
milestones.work: Euler, De linea brevissima in superficie quacunque duo quaelibet puncta jungente, Comm. Acad. Sci. Petropol. 3, pp. 110-124 (1732; written 1730), E9
milestones.description: Prompted by an exercise from Johann Bernoulli, Euler found the shortest line between two points on a surface analytically.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E9: published 1732, written 1730; summary says it arose from a task set by Bernoulli and gave early analytic foundations of the calculus of variations.

milestones.label: Clairaut on geodesics of surfaces of revolution
milestones.description: Clairaut published on the geodesics of quadrics of revolution, a topic Johann Bernoulli had also worked on.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Clairaut: in 1733 he published on geodesics of quadrics of rotation.

milestones.note: Exact publication not identified.

milestones.label: Mechanica vol. 2: geodesic equations from motion on a surface
milestones.work: Euler, Mechanica sive motus scientia analytice exposita, vol. 2, St Petersburg 1736, E16
milestones.description: Euler treated a point mass constrained to a surface and derived differential equations of geodesics from the mechanics, showing the free path is locally shortest.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E16: published 1736; summary says he derives differential equations of geodesics for free motion on a surface.

milestones.label: Methodus inveniendi treats geodesics in general
milestones.work: Euler, Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas..., 1744, E65
milestones.description: One of the worked problems of the general variational method is finding the geodesic on a given surface.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive E65 summary lists the geodesic joining two points on a given surface among the problems.

works.citation: Geodesics of quadrics of rotation (1733, per MacTutor)

notes: The summary's 'geodesic equation for motion on a surface' fits E16 (1736) rather than E9 (1732), which treats the shortest line by variational means; both are kept with separate roles. Johann Bernoulli's own geodesic results (late 1690s) were not verified in the pages read.
